Nothing in Kanae's carefree voice seemed to carry over from the other day.
Even so, I could not listen with an untroubled mind.

One memory called up another. The seeds of anguish threatened to sprout afresh.
I managed to suppress them; in their place, a weight of exhaustion like stone bore down on both shoulders.

en.html:
Captain Ootori let the sentence trail away.
Even converted into a signal, the hesitation remained in her voice and reached me intact.

Useful though the telephone was acknowledged to be, it had yet to become widespread.
Installation was expensive. So were the charges for using it.

I could hardly imagine those costs troubling Captain Ootori, who showed no sign of financial difficulty. Yet this was her first telephone call to me.
Usually, if she wanted something, she told me in person.

For her not to do so now, there ought to be a reason.

やや、言葉尻を濁す大鳥大尉。
　逡巡の様子は、音声の信号化を経ても消えず残って
伝わってきていた。

　電話はその利便性を認められながらも、まだ一般へ
の普及が進んでいるとは言えない機器だ。
　設置コストは高くつき、利用料金もまた同様である。

　経済的に困窮しているようには見えない大鳥大尉に
とってそれが重要な問題たるとは考えられなかったが、
電話を使って連絡を取ってきたのは今が初めてだった。
　彼女は大概、用があれば口頭で伝えてくる。

　今回そうしないからには、理由がある筈だ。

Kageaki"What work does a captain of the occupation army actually do?"

en.html:
Kenchoji, on Kofukusan, ranked first among the great temples known as the Five Mountains of Kamakura.
A Zen temple of long history, founded by Tokiyori Houjou, the Kamakura Shogunate's fifth regent.
Its school was Rinzai.

As one of Kamakura's principal temples, naturally I had visited it. That, however, was the extent of the connection.
Why I should go this instant, I could not imagine.

Whatever happened at Kenchoji ought to have been remote from me.

　建朝寺で何があるにしろ、自分とは遠い事柄の筈だ。

The news had been reported, if I remembered correctly, a day or two after the sword-offering visit to Hachimangu. ...That did not, however, rule out a connection between Moriuji Ashikaga's sudden death and the Prince.◆ Only now did I reach that thought. The Prince might have obtained an assassin in my place and carried it out. Had the Lord General been killed during the visit, such a fact could hardly be announced carelessly. An interval, followed by a report of mere 'sudden death,' would not contradict it. I had not seen for myself, but I had also heard that Hachimangu had been tightly sealed, for some reason, ever since the visit. ...Enough material to deepen the suspicion. One possibility, nevertheless. Nothing more. It was hard to imagine somebody conveniently available to the Prince as an assassin. At that point, I became aware of my own silence.
en.text:
I nodded at the Captain's words, odd as part of her intonation had been.
The news had been reported, if I remembered correctly, a day or two after the sword-offering visit to Hachimangu.

...That did not, however, rule out a connection between Moriuji Ashikaga's sudden death and the Prince.◆

Only now did I reach that thought.

The Prince might have obtained an assassin in my place and carried it out. Had the Lord General been killed during the visit, such a fact could hardly be announced carelessly. An interval, followed by a report of mere 'sudden death,' would not contradict it.

I had not seen for myself, but I had also heard that Hachimangu had been tightly sealed, for some reason, ever since the visit.
...Enough material to deepen the suspicion.

One possibility, nevertheless. Nothing more.
It was hard to imagine somebody conveniently available to the Prince as an assassin.
At that point, I became aware of my own silence.

en.html:
She ended the call.
I glared at the receiver, now carrying only a meaningless signal, then returned it to its cradle.

...What did it mean?
The Prince would be attacked? Because some scheme had gone wrong?

Had it indeed been the Prince who sent the Lord General to the underworld? Had Rokuhara discovered it and set out to retaliate?
Or was it less simple than that—

No.
This was no time to speculate over hidden circumstances.

If everything the Captain said was true, her last advice was right as well.
Only action remained.
